analysis.one_liner: Bans online services from selling subscribers' personal data without written consent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, after being referred there in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required internet and online service providers to get a subscriber's signed, informed written consent before sharing that subscriber's personal information with anyone else. Subscribers could revoke consent at any time, see and correct the data a company kept on them, and find out exactly who received it — all free of charge. The Federal Trade Commission could investigate violations and issue cease-and-desist orders, and subscribers could sue. It never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet subscribers, whose personal information could no longer be handed to third parties — advertisers, data brokers, or anyone else — without their signed consent. People could check what data was held about them, correct errors, revoke consent at any time, and sue for violations.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits an interactive computer service from disclosing a subscriber's personally identifiable information to any third party without the subscriber's prior informed written consent, and lets subscribers revoke that consent at any time.

Requires services, at a subscriber's request and without a fee, to show the subscriber the personal data held about them, let them verify and correct it, and disclose the identities of third parties who received it.

Bars services and their employees from knowingly disclosing personal information they have falsified, giving the Federal Trade Commission authority to investigate and issue cease-and-desist orders, and letting subscribers sue for relief.

analysis.who_pays: Internet and online service providers, which would lose the ability to compile and sell subscriber data without consent, and the data-marketing businesses that buy it. Compliance costs for consent tracking and subscriber access requests would fall on the companies.

drawbacks.text: The consent requirement and subscriber-access duties impose real compliance costs on online service providers, costs that could be passed to subscribers through higher service prices.

The bill applies only to 'interactive computer services' providing modem access to the Internet, a definition tied to dial-up era technology, so its protections could quickly lag behind how people actually connect and could create gaps between covered and uncovered services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — control over who receives your personal information — is substantial and enforceable through both the FTC and private lawsuits. The main weaknesses are the compliance burden on providers and the bill's dial-up-era definition of covered services, which would need updating over time. Weighing this honestly, the protections outweigh the costs for subscribers, though the definition would need repair.

outcome.mechanism: The House Commerce Committee referred it to its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection subcommittee three days after introduction, and it sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the Consumer Internet Privacy Protection Act of 1997 on January 7, 1997, the opening day of the 105th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce, and on January 22, 1997 to that committee's Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection.
It drew 15 cosponsors — 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but no further action was taken before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online service providers and the data-marketing businesses that wanted to compile and sell subscriber information were better off, since the bill died without restricting them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online service providers and data marketers

for.name: Rep. Bruce F. Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 7, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 13 of 205 House Democrats and 2 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing from both parties.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Rep. Thomas Bliley, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection subcommittee on January 22, 1997 and never brought it to a markup or floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans signing on, and the bill died quietly in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from disclosing subscribers' personal information to third parties without written consent and forced them to give subscribers access to and control over their data. Their business interest in monetizing subscriber data ran directly against subscribers' privacy. Note: this bill died in 1998, long before the modern data economy; the industry as it exists today was nascent then.

These businesses buy consumer information from service providers. The bill would have cut off consent-free flows of personally identifiable data to them, and required services to tell subscribers exactly who had received their information.
